summary: This document describes extensions to OSPF Traffic Engineering for carrying link performance information, such as propagation delay, which matters in networks like financial data feeds where path choice depends on it. Routers can then pick paths using these measures.

eli5.summary: Some networks, like stock-market feeds, care how fast a road is, not just whether it exists. This lets routers share how long each road takes so they choose the quickest.

questions: what is ospf te metric extension
what is the anomalous bit in ospf te
how does ospf advertise link bandwidth and loss
subtitle: New OSPF TE sub-TLVs that carry link delay, delay variation, loss and bandwidth so paths can be chosen by performance.

tldr.problem: In some networks, such as financial information networks, link performance such as propagation delay matters as much to path selection as other metrics. OSPF TE had no scalable way to distribute it.
tldr.mechanism: Seven new sub-TLVs (types 27 to 33) of the OSPF TE Link TLV carry delay, min/max delay, delay variation, loss, and residual, available and utilized bandwidth. An Anomalous bit flags threshold violations, and thresholds and timers limit how often values are flooded.
tldr.outcome: Other components can use the distributed data for path selection. Measuring the values and acting on them are outside the scope of the RFC.

today: RFC 7471 is a Proposed Standard from March 2015. The unit metadata shows it is not obsoleted or updated by any RFC and it updates none.

sections.title: Why Distribute Performance Data
sections.content:
In certain networks, such as financial information networks (for example stock market data providers), network performance information such as link propagation delay is becoming as critical to data path selection as other metrics. Hop count or cost then matter less. The RFC wants path decisions based on performance in a cost-effective and scalable way.

The extensions, called OSPF TE Metric Extensions, distribute link propagation delay, delay variation, link loss, residual bandwidth, available bandwidth and utilized bandwidth. They build on OSPFv2 TE (RFC 3630) and OSPFv3 TE (RFC 5329).

The data could replace cost with delay in routing, enhance Constrained Shortest Path First (CSPF), or feed a PCE or an ALTO server. With CSPF it can help set up, fail over and fail back paths using protocols such as RSVP-TE (RFC 3209). The RFC only covers distribution, not measurement or use.

A delay measurement SHOULD NOT vary significantly with offered load, and so SHOULD NOT include queuing delays.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the shortest road is not the fastest. This lets towns share how fast each road really is.

sections.title: New Sub-TLVs and the Anomalous Bit
sections.content:
OSPFv2 TE LSAs are opaque LSAs with area flooding scope. OSPFv3 Intra-Area-TE-LSAs have their own LSA type, also with area flooding scope. Both hold a single TLV with nested sub-TLVs, and the Link TLV, common to both, describes a link between OSPF neighbors. This RFC adds seven sub-TLVs to the Link TLV.

Many of them carry an Anomalous (A) bit. When it is clear, the sub-TLV describes steady state link performance, which could be used to build a steady state topology for initial tunnel path computation or to verify failover paths. When performance violates configurable link-local thresholds, a sub-TLV with the A bit set is advertised. An ingress node can then check whether the link affects its LSPs, whether those LSPs still meet end-to-end objectives, and if not move traffic to a protection LSP or build a new one.

If performance later improves past a configurable reuse threshold, the sub-TLV can be re-advertised with the bit cleared. The A bit was intentionally left out of some sub-TLVs to help mitigate oscillations.

Delay, delay variation and loss MUST be encoded as integers. Bandwidths MUST be IEEE single precision floating point. Delay and variation are in microseconds, loss is a percentage, and bandwidth is in bytes per second. All values except residual bandwidth MUST be rolling averages over a configurable period.
sections.eli5: Each road report can carry a red flag meaning it is much worse than usual. When the road recovers, the flag comes down.

sections.title: Delay, Variation and Loss Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
All values describe the direction from the advertising node to its neighbor. The delay sub-TLVs have a 24-bit field in microseconds.

  • Unidirectional Link Delay (type 27, length 4): the average link delay over a configurable interval. The maximum value 16,777,215 means the delay is at least that value and may be larger.
  • Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay (type 28, length 8): the minimum and maximum measured delay over a configurable interval. Implementations MAY allow a configured offset to be added to advertise operator specific constraints.
  • Unidirectional Delay Variation (type 29, length 4): average delay variation, with no A bit. A value of 0 means it has not been measured.
  • Unidirectional Link Loss (type 30, length 4): packet loss as a percentage of traffic sent. The basic unit is 0.000003%, and (2^24 - 2) is 50.331642%, the highest expressible value. Larger measured values SHOULD be encoded as the maximum.

Reserved bits MUST be set to 0 when sent and ignored when received. The RFC reasons that high speed links with over 50% loss are unusable.
sections.eli5: These reports say how long the trip takes, how much it wobbles, and how many packages get lost on the way.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
Three sub-TLVs, each of length 4, carry a bandwidth as a floating point number in bytes per second. They apply to a link, forwarding adjacency, or bundled link, and for a bundled link the value is the sum over the component links.

  • Residual Bandwidth (type 31): Maximum Bandwidth minus the bandwidth currently allocated to RSVP-TE LSPs.
  • Available Bandwidth (type 32): residual bandwidth minus the measured bandwidth used to forward non-RSVP-TE LSP packets.
  • Utilized Bandwidth (type 33): the actual utilization of the link, as measured by the advertising node.

Residual Bandwidth differs from Unreserved Bandwidth of RFC 3630. Residual subtracts tunnel reservations from the link capacity and gives one aggregated remainder. Unreserved is taken from the Maximum Reservable Bandwidth and gives per priority remainders. They can be used together, for example the former for Weighted ECMP and the latter for call admission control.
sections.eli5: One note says how much of the road is free of reserved lanes, one says how much is really free right now, and one says how much is in use.

sections.title: Thresholds, Suppression and Stability
sections.content:
Advertised values (except min/max delay and residual bandwidth) MUST be averages or come from a filter such as a rolling average. Measurement intervals, filter coefficients and advertisement intervals MUST be configurable for each sub-TLV. Implementations SHOULD provide accelerated advertisement thresholds: if a value crosses a configured bound, or differs from the last advertised value by more than a threshold, the advertisement is made immediately. To prevent oscillation, only the high or the low threshold, not both, may trigger a given sub-TLV.

Small changes below the thresholds SHOULD be suppressed or refreshed less often. Instability might occur in very large networks if measurement intervals overwhelm the processing of flooded information. The default measurement interval should be 30 seconds, the minimum announcement periodicity is 1 announcement per second, the default inter-update timer should be 120 seconds, and it should not be lower than the measurement interval.

Implementations MUST allow each sub-TLV to be enabled or disabled individually, and SHOULD allow static configuration or manual override of measurements to ease migration.
sections.eli5: To stop everyone shouting every second, reports go out on a schedule. Only a big change gets announced right away.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
As in RFC 3630, an unrecognized TLV should be silently ignored: not processed, but included in LSAs sent to OSPF neighbors. So routers that do not know the new sub-TLVs are not broken by them.

The document introduces no security issues beyond those of RFC 3630. It points to extra protection from OSPFv2 HMAC-SHA (RFC 5709), OSPFv3 IPsec (RFC 4552) and the OSPFv3 Authentication Trailer (RFC 7166), and to the KARP analysis in RFC 6863.
sections.eli5: Routers that do not understand the new notes just pass them along. The safety rules are the same as before.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 on send, ignored on receipt.
